newsitem.title: USA: S&P sees Venezuela recovering from banking crisis.
newsitem.headline: S&P sees Venezuela recovering from banking crisis.

text.p: Standard & Poor's on Monday said it believes the Venezuelan government's commitment to economic reforms will release the country from the effects of its devastating banking crisis of 1994 and 1995.
Furthermore, S&P said sovereign ratings are poised to improve should reforms continue as expected.

"Standard & Poor's does not believe that the Venezuelan financial system will weigh any longer on its sovereign rating, and this could allow for an eventual amelioration of the rating should broader reforms move forward," S&P said.
The ratings agency said its brighter outlook is based on its belief that decisive government action could stunt damage from any future bank failures.

In addition, S&P said the expected privatizations of Banco de Venezuela and Banco Consolidado underscore the government's commitment to economic reform and should introduce "much needed competition to the financial sector."
For all the improvements, however, S&P noted the Venezuelan banking sector is still characterized by high risk compared with other Latin American banking systems.

That risk will remain high, S&P said, until the banks can resume their normal role as lenders of funds rather than as holders of government bills; until the banks can regain public confidence and capture more of depositors' total savings; and until regulatory norms can be strengthened on loan grading, offshore supervision and sanctioning.
Venezuela's banking crisis had contributed to a series of S&P downgrades of the republic's sovereign rating to the current single-B from BB in March 1994, S&P said.
S&P analysts John Chambers and Ursula Wilhelm made the comments in the most recent issue of the agency's Creditweek publication.
